name: Tomas Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers are confidential. What does your workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Tomas Rahman, 58, and I came to the electricity company after driving deliveries. With a vocational certificate I'm a junior lineworker: I check truck stock, help build and repair power lines, and ask my senior partner Ravi about difficult cable joints; restoring a street is satisfying, but I still move slowly at an unfamiliar pole.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What helps you get it right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A clear circuit sheet and a second pair of eyes from my senior workmate Ravi help me get it right. I haven't used AI tools, and I don't want a polished screen answer to replace a measured voltage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quicker work order is fine if we can still read it in the rain. The line doesn't repair itself because someone has found a clever way to type.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't expect much change to my day. I took the certificate at 55 after driving deliveries, so I'm still learning the line trade; a high wage and almost a year's expenses saved give me time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll continue the assigned pole and cable jobs with my senior partner checking the tricky parts. In the first year I'll keep the printed circuit list in the truck and continue the same monthly transfer to our savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel quiet about it. My partner Inez and I have grown children and a manageable house payment, so a little office automation doesn't rearrange our supper table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the printed list help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the tablet battery failed beside a roadside transformer. The truck copy had the circuit number, and our supervisor confirmed it before we began.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone urge you to try an AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger workers do, but I haven't used one. I'd rather ask my senior partner Ravi to explain a cable joint while I can see the actual parts.

say: I'd say **clear work orders** matter more than faster typing.
I'd remind coworkers the **line repair** still needs trained hands.
think: My **junior skills** need more practice despite the higher rate.
Nearly a **year of savings** makes a small office change harmless to our budget.
do: Continue **assigned repairs** with Ravi supervising difficult joints.
Keep the **printed circuit list** in the truck and maintain normal savings transfers.
feel: **Quietly secure** about work and household money.
S0.quote: The line doesn't repair itself because someone has found a clever way to type.
fieldNote: Tomas's **printed circuit list** has already proved useful during a battery failure, reinforcing his preference for familiar backups.
His **higher wage and savings** support calm, though he remains junior after entering line work from deliveries.

steps.text: Continue assigned pole and cable repairs with Ravi supervising difficult joints

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the office to try the planning system on real winter calls before cutting any dispatcher. Fast routes are useful only if the crew receives the right circuit and safe access point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the physical repair part to last, since robots spread slowly in this picture. I do worry the company could tighten the roster and remove callout hours; Inez works a steady library desk, but our house payment still comes each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the dispatcher to show me one new route beside the paper feeder map, without pretending I know the software. In the first year I'd keep taking field shifts and stop booking our annual coastal week if callout pay falls for two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy about the roster, and wary of a screen that hides an error behind a clean map. I don't object to a tested improvement; I just need to see it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to see on that winter call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The access gate behind the grain store locks in snow, so the route needs the south lane. A dispatcher knows that; a map might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does losing a coastal week mean to Inez?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be disappointed, and so would I. Still, that trip is easier to postpone than a house payment if the extra calls slow down.

say: I'd ask for **winter-call tests** before dispatch posts change.
I'd say **safe access points** matter as much as route speed.
think: My **field repairs** remain for now, but callout hours could shrink.
Our **house payment** makes even a modest overtime cut noticeable.
do: Compare one **new route** with the paper feeder map and dispatcher's advice.
Keep **field shifts** and postpone the coastal week after two months of lower callout pay.
feel: **Uneasy** about roster changes and hidden map errors.
S1.quote: Fast routes are useful only if the crew receives the right circuit and safe access point.
fieldNote: Tomas's **risk is overtime**, not immediate replacement of physical repair work under slower robot adoption.
He will inspect a **real route** with a dispatcher, while declining to claim expertise with software he never uses.

steps.text: Keep taking paid line repair shifts during roster changes
Postpone the coastal holiday after two months of lower callout pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot that 2028 thinking AI will alter plans, but robots don't reach the pole until about 2031. I want a named person responsible for each isolation, whatever the machine says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, I might still need this wage and could be a junior name on a cut list. We have nearly a year saved and other utilities nearby, but I don't know if they would hire someone who started the trade late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask the company for a written account of how junior posts would change and get my work record in order. In 2029 I'd apply to two nearby utilities if cuts look likely; during the first robot year I'd keep applying for paid line or equipment-checking work, and use savings only to bridge the search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about that short clock. I have a plan, but it depends on real employers rather than a promise from a machine seller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Inez hear at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Inez the truth. We're not treating savings as a pension. Our grown sons have rent and families of their own, so we won't put the problem on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a paid equipment-checking course if an employer showed a recognised job at the end. I wouldn't buy a private course just because a brochure called it the future.

say: I'd separate **2028 planning AI** from 2031 field robots.
I'd demand a **named safety lead** for every isolation.
think: At **63**, I may still need wages when junior posts are cut.
Nearby utilities offer **possibilities**, not a guaranteed hire for a late starter.
do: Request a **written staffing account** and prepare my work record now.
Apply to **nearby utilities** in 2029 if cuts loom; keep seeking paid line or equipment-checking work in 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about the short clock, with a practical search plan.
S2.quote: We're not treating savings as a pension.
fieldNote: Tomas distinguishes **2028 plans** from the 2031 robot threat to his physical repair income.
His **job search** is conditional on credible cuts; he refuses to treat nearly a year's savings as lasting retirement income.

steps.text: Request written junior staffing plans before deciding on applications
Apply to nearby utilities in 2029 if field cuts look likely
Take a paid equipment-checking course if a recognised job follows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make management show us a safe trial and a staffing plan. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and field robots around 2034, so the line crew should be involved long before the second date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 66 when robots can do repairs, and I may be ready to stop climbing by then. I won't assume retirement works until Inez and I see the figures for our house payment and living costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request a retirement estimate and speak at the company's safety meeting about isolation sign-offs. In 2032 I'd put a modest extra amount from overtime toward the remaining house loan; when robots arrive in 2034 I'd retire if the written figures cover us, or apply for an equipment-checking shift if they don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less cornered than in the fast one. There is time to check the books and the machine, though I still dislike having to trust a trial run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra would go to the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe fifty from an overtime pay packet, only when the callout actually happens. Inez would rather keep our emergency savings intact than make a big payment from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe trial show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see a robot stop when the label and the measured voltage disagree. Someone from the crew should sign the record, not only the supplier.

say: I'd request a **safe trial** and a staffing plan before 2034 robots.
I'd explain **2031 thinking AI** changes plans before field repairs change.
think: At **66**, retirement may be possible but needs household figures.
Our **house payment** remains a real cost when deciding whether to stop climbing.
do: Get a **retirement estimate** and speak about isolation at the company safety meeting.
Pay **fifty from actual overtime** toward the house loan, then choose retirement or equipment-checking work in 2034.
feel: **Less cornered**, though still wary of unproven robot trials.
S3.quote: Someone from the crew should sign the record, not only the supplier.
fieldNote: Tomas's **2034 decision** turns on verified income and the remaining house payment, not a guessed retirement age.
He supports **measured-voltage trials** and puts only earned overtime toward debt, keeping emergency savings intact.

steps.text: Pay fifty from each actual overtime packet toward the house loan
Compare written retirement income with house and living costs
Apply for equipment-checking shifts in 2034 if retirement falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger crew to keep proper circuit records for the next decade, because they will work beside the robots longer than I will. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 and field robots in 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to have left climbing before 71 if our retirement estimate and house payment line up. The extra time feels useful, though Inez's library desk work could change with thinking AI in 2036 and that needs a place in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep paid line shifts and get written estimates for both our retirement incomes. In 2037 we'd choose a date to stop my climbing work if the bills fit, and in 2039 I'd give Ravi my paper notes on troublesome circuits before any robot uses the new map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own work over the next few years and thoughtful about Inez's job later. A decade means we can adjust the plan before the bills force us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be in Ravi's notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Ridge Street transformer has a faded tag that looks like a different circuit in low light. I'd mark the photograph and the correct number on paper before passing it along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Inez's hours fall before retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd delay my retirement date and work through the budget again. Our savings help, but neither of us wants a date we can't afford.

say: I'd urge younger crews to keep **proper circuit records** for the decade ahead.
I'd note **2039 field robots** arrive when I'll be 71.
think: I expect to leave **climbing work** before robots arrive if our figures hold.
Inez's **library hours** could change in 2036 and alter our retirement budget.
do: Keep **paid line shifts** and obtain written estimates for both retirement incomes.
Choose a **2037 departure date** if bills fit; pass troublesome circuit notes to Ravi in 2039.
feel: **Calm** about near-term wages, thoughtful about Inez's later income.
S4.quote: Our savings help, but neither of us wants a date we can't afford.
fieldNote: Tomas expects **field wages through preparation**, with retirement before 2039 conditional on both partners' income figures.
His **paper circuit notes** preserve a specific hazard for Ravi and later robot use, consistent with his familiar-work preference.

steps.text: Keep paid line shifts while obtaining both retirement income estimates
Choose a 2037 departure date only if household bills fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots arrive in 2031, when I might still need the wage and still be a junior in this trade. A written staffing plan, paid recognised training, real openings nearby and crew-signed safety tests would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the circuit number when a screen and a faded pole tag disagree. The wrong number isn't an argument; it can hurt someone.

headlineQuote: The wrong number isn't an argument; it can hurt someone.
portrait: Tomas is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who entered from delivery driving and still relies on Ravi for difficult cable joints.
His **higher wage and savings** provide a buffer, but a house payment means he still needs reliable paid work.
He **never uses AI tools** and favours printed circuit records, measured voltage and crew-signed equipment trials.
The fast scenario's **2031 robots** worry him most because his late start and junior standing could limit replacement work.
Longer warning lets him **check retirement figures**, reduce house debt from actual overtime and preserve field notes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Tomas most because 2031 robots could reach his job while he still needs wages.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **written staffing plan**, paid recognised training, local openings and crew-signed safety trials.
